results.title: How to create and use a causal diagram (DAG) – Causal Diagrams
results.content: # How to create and use a causal diagram (DAG). A causal diagram, or causal ‘directed acyclic graph’ (DAG), is a cognitive tool that can help you identify and avoid, or at least understand and acknowledge, some potential sources of bias that might alter your study’s findings. Specify/define the exposure (variable of interest) and the outcome as precisely as possible, including when their values have been or will be determined. Draw an arrow between any variables thought likely to be causally associated; indicating the direction of the causal relationship with the direction favouring the stronger causal effect if the variables affect each other over time but it is not clear which variable was determined earlier in the data. Other guides and sources of information on how to create and use a causal diagram include:. Use of directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) to identify confounders in applied health research: review and recommendations. Directed acyclic graphs: a tool for causal studies in paediatrics.

results.content: # Confounders, mediators, moderators and covariates. I started looking for some nice examples that would describe what a mediator was. Of course, it was also important to pre-empt confusion between similar and related terms, and since mediators and confounders are regularly mixed up I also looked for nice examples of confounders. For completeness I looked for examples of moderators and covariates. Mediators and confounders are similar except for the direction of effect between them and the exposure/treatment. Mediators are additionally characterised by lying on the causal pathway between exposure and outcome. Moderators are simply interaction terms that change the size or direction (or both) of the effect of the exposure on outcome. The confusion between mediators and confounders arises from the fact that both have associations between the exposure and outcome. 1. I know that Pearl's Structured Causal Models (SCMs) are directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). However, it seems that these two paradigms should be able to be brought together given that they bought model causal relationships through graphs. It seems that are slightly less quantitative but could easily be parameterized by adding a function between the nodes in the CLD similar to how SCMs work. asked Apr 4, 2024 at 20:36. ## 1 Answer 1. For one, causal loop diagrams are cyclic, whereas SCMs are based on acyclic graphs, so that's not an easy gap to bridge. Moreover, SCMs describe a data-generating process which can be visualized as a graph, whereas CLDs seem to be something of a visualization tool for an underlying dynamic system, or to express background knowledge without explicitly modeling the system, which comes at the risk of imprecision and misunderstandings. That said, there are versions of SCMs that incorporate feedback loops, and they may me compatible with the dynamical systems underlying CLDs. This list focuses on end-user software tools which allow drawing and editing of Causal Diagrams and DAGs. CausalWizard is a **browser-based** web-app which provides Causal Diagram editing (although you can interpret your diagram as an ordinary DAG) and can also perform causal effect estimation with your data, by first identifying causal effects with adjustment sets or instrumental variables and then fitting various machine learning models. * **TETRAD** is a **free**, Java-based tool for creating and analyzing causal diagrams, DAGs, and **undirected** graphs. **DAGitty** **and** **CausalWizard** **both stand out as browser-based, free platforms that will allow you to freely draw causal diagrams and DAGs.** Of the two, we think CausalWizard is easier to use, but we’re biased :) .

results.title: Causal Inference and DAGs: Glasses to See the Hidden Truth | by Eric Morales Mora | Medium
results.content: # Causal Inference and DAGs: Glasses to See the Hidden Truth. For example, you know the relationship between drinking alcohol and getting drunk: while drinking alcohol causes drunkenness (causation), simply observing people at a party with drinks in their hands doesn’t mean they’re all drunk (association). If you are a data analysis addict like me, you probably need to be aware of the power of Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) as tools for navigating complex causal relationships. The technological ability to make personal measurements of exposures — toxicants, physical agents, or other variables — is rapidly advancing (yes, I’m an environmental epidemiology practitioner). Using simple rules, DAGs help researchers identify confounding variables and determine which should be controlled to eliminate bias. Let’s explore the three fundamental structures in causal diagrams using the example of drinking alcohol and getting drunk:. * If we hold B constant (*e.g.,* no alcohol in the bloodstream), A (drinking alcohol) will not lead to C (getting drunk). * If we hold B constant (*e.g*., everyone at the same event), A (drinking alcohol) and C (getting drunk) become independent. If we condition on Being observed (B), drinking alcohol and social event assistance may appear inversely related (*e.g.,* those being observed might drink but not attend a social event). ## Hidden Connections in Causal Diagrams. Causal diagrams help identify direct relationships and reveal hidden connections or confounding factors that might mislead our interpretation of data. Consider the relationship between drinking alcohol (X) and getting drunk (Y). While there is an apparent causal link, a hidden confounder, such as the social environment (L), could introduce bias. Let’s say social events (L) are associated with both drinking alcohol (X) and getting drunk (Y). By identifying and properly controlling confounders in our causal diagrams, we can isolate the true causal effect, ensuring our interpretations are valid and actionable. Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) offer a powerful lens — our “secret glasses” — to help us navigate the complexities of causal relationships. Whether it’s the influence of alcohol in the bloodstream on drunkenness or the role of social events as hidden confounders, DAGs remind us that causality isn’t always visible on the surface.
